newsitem.title: JAPAN: Bruised dollar dips below 113 yen in late Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: Bruised dollar dips below 113 yen in late Tokyo.

text.p: 0625 GMT TRADED HI/LO AS OF 0600 GMT
The bruised dollar dipped below 113 yen in late Tokyo trade after falling nearly three full yen from its New York close and dealers said more falls are likely.

Stop-loss selling in morning trade was augmented by panic sales, with sharp slides against the yen in cross-trading on institutional investor hedge sales also undermining the dollar. By 0632 GMT it had touched a low of around 112.80 yen.
Dealers said that the selling appears to be far from over, with long positions still remaining in the market and European trading yet to begin in earnest.
"We may see some technical support near 112 yen, but it is very weak. The next support point under that is 111.50 yen and then 111.00 yen flat," one said.

Although the market is still watching avidly for the outcome of today's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, many dealers said they felt it was unlikely that any sustained support will result from this even if interest rates are raised.

One trust bank dealer said that, while the dollar could rebound on any rate rise, its gains were likely to be limited to 115 yen at best, with profit-taking sales at that point. "If they don't raise rates, dollar sales will start at whatever level it is at when the results are announced," he added.
The dollar was hovering around 113 yen in late Tokyo after gaining slightly on short-covering and some light bids from Japanese operators, but most dealers said this was temporary.
The greenback began its slide in morning Tokyo trade as waves of stop-loss selling were set off on expectations that the U.S.-Japan interest rate gap may shrink.

NHK television reported early Tuesday that Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party will make a recommendation to Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto by the end of the month that Japan raise its official discount rate. Speculation has also risen that the FOMC will leave U.S. rates unchanged.

Growing U.S. concern about rises in Japan's trade surplus also weighed on the dollar after U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said on Monday that a sustained increase in Japan's current account surplus would be a "very serious problem."
Japan's overall customs-cleared trade surplus grew 163.7 percent to 831.48 billion yen in April.

Although dollar sales appeared to have eased slightly in the early afternoon, selling picked up again as the yen gained sharply in cross-trading, rising particularly strongly against the mark, Swiss franc and sterling.

Some dealers said that institutional investors, particularly trust banks, were selling various currencies for the yen to hedge against further losses in their foreign assets, although other dealers said they were unsure of this.
But no such selling was detected as yet from Japan's cash-rich life insurers, one trust bank dealer said.
Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the International Finance Bureau at the Ministry of Finance, declined to comment on the current dollar/yen rate.

Some dealers said stop-loss sell orders could emerge at every 0.50 yen fall of the dollar, with no real support until the important psychological support level of 110 yen. "Right now, there's nothing to do but wait for a good chance to sell," one dealer said.
